title: Count how many times a given number appears in an array (loop + counter).
shortTitle: Count how many times a given number appears in an array
keyPoints: Walk the array once with a counter and increment it each time an element matches the target value.
There is no early exit because the target can appear multiple times anywhere in the array.
For money compare with compareTo returning zero, not equals, because equals also checks scale.
Time complexity is O(n) and space complexity is O(1) regardless of how many matches exist.
This pattern is the foundation for frequency counting, histogram building, and detecting recurring charges.
For sorted arrays, binary search can find the first and last occurrence in O(log n) to compute the count without a full scan.

s1_definition.oneliner: Walk the array once with a counter, and add one to the counter every time an element matches the target.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Linear scan** – visit every element because the target can appear anywhere, giving O(n) time.
- **Counter variable** – a single `int count` tracks matches, giving O(1) extra space.
- **No early exit** – unlike existence checks, counting requires inspecting every element.
- **Value equality** – for `BigDecimal` use `compareTo` returning zero, not `equals`, because `equals` also checks scale.
- **Result** – the counter holds the total number of occurrences when the loop ends.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh wants to know how many times exactly Rs.5000 was debited from his account SAV2001 this month, perhaps a recurring subscription. He reads each transaction in his passbook, and every time the amount is exactly Rs.5000 he makes a tally mark. At the end, the number of tally marks is the count.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Counting how many times a value appears in an array is a straightforward linear scan with a counter. I start a counter at zero, loop through every element, and increment the counter each time the element matches the target. There is no early exit because the target can appear anywhere, so I must inspect every element.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used this to build a recurring charge detector. Rajesh wanted to know how many times exactly five thousand rupees was debited this month so he could spot a subscription he forgot about. I loop through his transaction amounts and tally each one that equals five thousand.

The important nuance here is how I compare money. I compare BigDecimal values using the compareTo method and check for a result of zero, rather than using the equals method. The reason is that five thousand written as plain five thousand and five thousand written with two decimal places are the same amount of money, but the equals method considers them different because their scale differs. By using compareTo I treat them as equal in value, which is exactly what the customer means.

Remember one sentence: walk every element, compare with compareTo for BigDecimal, and increment the counter on each match.
